The six grammatical relations (kārakas) and their connection are of two kinds, according to whether they are expressed or unexpressed; and the case-ending (vibhakti) must also be determined—this is certain for one who desires correct application [of grammar]. (2)
Whatever cognition has arisen regarding something, or whatever compound may exist therein— that very thing, when being employed, expresses [its object] by means of its gender and number.
The application of gender and number is generally observed,
as is the usage "the Vedas are the authority" (vedāḥ pramāṇam) and so forth, which is accepted by him.
The suffix denotes the primary agent when there are multiple agents;
the primary instigator is to be understood as such if he was not himself instigated by others. (5)
The secondary object of roots such as *duh* (to milk) and the primary object of roots such as *nī* (to lead) and *vah* (to carry) [is expressed by the accusative];
however, the suffix born of the object (*karmaja*) expresses only the agent or the object when the root ends in *-in*, or else something other than those two.

In verbal roots ending in *ani*, the meanings are "going," "eating," and "understanding"; the word-meanings [of such roots] function as the object (*karman*) when they are intransitive, but as the agent (*kartṛ*) when they are transitive. (7)
The roots *nī*, *khād*, and others do not have the agent as the object;
likewise, *bhakṣ* does not [have the agent as the object] when it means "eating," and *vah* has the charioteer as its agent.
Likewise, for the roots *hṛ* (to take) and *kṛ* (to do), the agent may be either the object or the subject;
similarly, for *abhivad* (to salute) and *dṛś* (to see), the same applies when used in a reflexive sense.
That which is not mentioned would be other than what has been stated; for the first [case-ending] alone would indeed be used for what is stated.
However, when it is unstated, the others—the second and so forth—occur as appropriate.
The third case ending shall occur for the agentive factor (kartṛ), and the second case ending for the objective factor (karma).
Furthermore, the sixth case ending may occur for those two [factors] when they are not associated with a verbal derivative (kṛt) ending in a past participle suffix (niṣṭhā) or the like.
When a single [kāraka] is assigned [the status of agent], the genitive occurs for the action alone and not for the agent;
however, when the suffix *akā* is not employed, the genitive may be used for both.
Generally, only those [verbs] are seen where the agent and the object are expressed according to their designations;
as for others, their occurrence has not been excluded. (13)
The third case is generally used for the instrument; the fourth for the recipient;
the fifth occurs for the source of separation; and likewise, the seventh for the locus. (14)

Now, regarding the relation [of the suffix], the genitive case (ṣaṣṭhī) may occur; such is the determination through the investigation of what has been stated and what has not been stated. Therefore, let its usage be understood accordingly. (15)
I bow down to that Buddha, by whom the naked army of Māra and the cage of existence were conquered, and who has ascended to the state of Nirvāṇa. || 1 ||

The expressed agent; the unexpressed agent. The expressed object; the unexpressed object. The expressed instrument; the unexpressed instrument. The expressed recipient; the unexpressed recipient. The expressed ablative; the unexpressed ablative. The expressed locus; the unexpressed locus. The expressed relation; the unexpressed relation.

Thus, the agent is expressed there, as in the following examples: *jayati buddhadharmaḥ* (the Buddha-dharma triumphs), *jvalati hutāśanaḥ* (the fire blazes), *edhate vidhuḥ* (the moon waxes), *kārako devadattaḥ* (Devadatta is the doer), *vaiyākaraṇaḥ puruṣaḥ* (the man is a grammarian), and *kṛtapraṇāmaḥ puruṣaḥ* (the man by whom a salutation was made). In such cases, because verbal suffixes (*ākhyāta*), primary suffixes (*kṛt*), secondary suffixes (*taddhita*), and compounds are prescribed with reference to the agent (*kartṛ*), it is said that "the agent is expressed. By the rule that "when the agent is expressed, the nominative case (*prathamā*) is used," the nominative case is employed.

When the agent (*kartṛ*) is not expressed, [the third case ending] is used: *jīyate buddhadharmeṇa* ("he is conquered by the Buddha-dharma"), *jvalyate hutāśanena* ("it is made to blaze by fire"), *aidhyate vidhunā* ("it is kindled by the wind"), *kṛtaṃ devadattena* ("done by Devadatta"). Even in the case of a transitive verb (*sakarmaka*), if the object (*karman*) is not intended to be expressed, then the suffix denotes the abstract state (*bhāva*). In such examples as these, since the suffix is not prescribed for the agent, the third case ending is employed for the agent because it is unexpressed (*anukta*). As for the expressed object (*uktaṃ karma*), for example:

"A mat is being made" (*kaṭaḥ kriyate*), "rice is being cooked" (*odanaḥ pacyate*), "the village is being gone to" (*grāmo gamyate*), "rice has been eaten" (*bhukta odanaḥ*), "a cloth worth a hundred" (*śatikaḥ paṭaḥ*), "a tree climbed by a monkey" (*āruḍhavānaro vṛkṣaḥ*). In such examples, because the suffixes and the compounds are prescribed for the expressed object (*karmavihitatvāt*), it is said that "the first case [ending] expresses the object. This is according to the rule: "When the object is expressed, the first case [ending is used]. An unexpressed object (*anuktaṃ karma*) is as follows: "He makes a mat" (*kaṭaṃ karoti*), "He cooks rice" (*odanaṃ pacati*), "He goes to the village" (*grāmaṃ gacchati*), "He has eaten rice" (*odanaṃ bhuktavān*). In such examples, since the suffix is not prescribed for the object, the second case ending is used for the object because it is unexpressed.

The expressed instrument (*karaṇa*) is as follows: *snānīyaṃ varṇam* (the color for bathing). Its meaning is: that color by which one bathes is "bathing-color" (*snānīya*). This is according to the rule: "The suffixes *kṛtya* and *uṭ* occur even in meanings other than those [specifically taught]. The suffix *anīya* occurs in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇa*). Such examples are called "expressed instruments"; because it is expressed, the nominative case is used for the instrument.
An unexpressed instrument (*anukta-karaṇa*) is as follows:

One bathes with color; one cuts with a sword; one goes to Mount Meru by means of the mind. Alternatively, in cases such as "one is bathed by color," "it is cut by a sword," or "it is gone to by the mind," since no suffix has been prescribed for the instrumental (karaṇa) case, the third case ending is applied to the instrumental because it has not been [otherwise] stated.
The recipient (saṃpradāna) has been explained.

For example, "a Brāhmaṇa worthy of a gift" (*dānīya*). This is the meaning: that to whom a gift is given is called *dānīya*. By the rule "the suffixes *kṛtya* and *uṭ* are used even in other senses," the suffix *anīya* is applied here in the sense of the recipient (*saṃpradāna*). Likewise, "a Brāhmaṇa worthy of a sacrificial fee" (*dakṣiṇīya*). That to whom a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is given is *dakṣiṇīya*. Here, by the separation of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) "the suffix *īya* is used in the sense of 'beneficial'," the suffix *īya* is applied here in the sense of the recipient. Similarly, "a guest who has been fed" (*dattabhojana*). Since the compound here is formed with the recipient as the prior member, the nominative case is used for the recipient because it has already been stated [in such examples]. An unstated recipient is as follows:

"He gives to the Brāhmaṇa" (*dadāti brāhmaṇāya*), or "it is given to the Brāhmaṇa" (*dīyate brāhmaṇāya*); likewise, "it should be given to the Brāhmaṇa" (*dātavyaṃ brāhmaṇāya*). In such cases, since the suffix is not prescribed for the *saṃpradāna* (recipient) case, the fourth case (*caturthī*) is employed because it has not been [otherwise] stated. The *apādāna* (ablative/source) has been explained: "the terrifying Rākṣasa" (*bhīmo rākṣasaḥ*). He is called *bhīma* because one fears him (*bibhetyasmāt*). In the rule "bhīmādayo 'pādāne," the suffix *mak* is added to the roots *bhī* and *bhīṣi* according to the *Uṇādi* sūtras. Similarly, "the land of Uśinara" (*uśan ajanapadaḥ*) is a compound in the sense of the *apādāna*. Because these have been stated in such contexts, the first case (*prathamā*) is used for the *apādāna*.
An example of an unstated ablative (*apādāna*) is:

*bibheti rākṣasāt* ("he fears the rākṣasa") or *bhīyate rākṣasāt* ("he is feared by the rākṣasa"). Likewise: *bhīto rākṣasāt* ("frightened from the rākṣasa"). Since no specific suffix has been prescribed for the ablative here, the fifth case (*pañcamī*) is used for the ablative because it is unstated.
An example of a stated locative (*adhikaraṇa*) is as follows:

*Āsanaṃ* means a seat (*pīṭha*). This is the meaning: that upon which one sits is a *āsana*. By the rule *karaṇādhikaraṇayośca*, the suffix *yuṭ* is applied in the sense of locus (*adhikaraṇa*). Similarly, *vaṭakinī* refers to the full-moon day (*pūrṇimāsī*); on that full-moon day, *vaṭaka* cakes are generally eaten. Here, the suffix *in* is used according to conventional usage (*ruḍhi*). Likewise, in the compound *mattamātaṅgaṃ vanaṃ* (the forest of intoxicated elephants), the accusative case is used for the locus because it has been so stated in such instances. An example of an unstated locus is as follows:

"He sits on the seat" (āste pīṭhe), or "He is seated on the seat" (āsyate pīṭhe); likewise, "It has been sat upon by him on the seat" (evamāsitaṃ pīṭhe). "A hamlet on the Ganges" (gaṅgāyāṃ ghoṣaḥ), "oil in sesame seeds" (tileṣu tailam), "gods in heaven" (divi devāḥ)—in such cases as these, no suffix is prescribed for the locus (*adhikaraṇa*). Thus, because it is not [otherwise] stated, the locative case (*saptamī*) is used for the locus. Regarding what is already expressed (*ukta*), an example of a relationship (*saṃbandha*) is:

"Devadatta is possessed of cows" (*gomān devadattaḥ*). The meaning is this: he to whom cows belong is "possessed of cows" (*gomān*). In the sense of the relationship "that belongs to him," the possessive suffix *matup* is applied. Similarly, "Devadatta is the owner of brindled cows" (*citragur devadattaḥ*)—here, the compound (*samāsa*) occurs in the sense of a relationship. Therefore, in such instances, because the relationship is already expressed, the nominative case (*prathamā*) is used.

An example of an unexpressed relation (*anukta-sambandha*) is as follows: *gāvo vidyante yasya devadattasya* ("the cows belong to Devadatta"), or *gobhir vidyate devadattasya* ("Devadatta possesses cows"). Similarly: *rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ* ("the king's man") and *vṛkṣasya śākhā* ("the tree's branch"). In such cases, the genitive case is used because the relation is not expressed by any other means. This is merely an illustration of both expressed and unexpressed relations; we shall provide a detailed exposition of them in their proper places later on. Now, who indeed speaks of both the six factors of action (*kāraka-ṣaṭka*) and the relation?

Whatever cognition has arisen regarding something, or whatever compound may exist therein, that very [cognition] expresses it by means of its gender and number as one who is engaged [in the act of speaking]. (3)

"Whichever [suffix] in whichever [meaning]," and so forth. This is the meaning: whichever suffix—whether a *taddhita* such as *-tya* and so on, or a *kṛt* suffix—is not [already] produced in a particular meaning, case-role (*kāraka*), or relation; and in whichever meaning a compound (*samāsa*) occurs—that suffix and that compound express that very meaning in which they are prescribed. To the question "Being of what nature does it express it?", he says:

"Being joined" (*yuñjānaḥ*) means being connected with the gender—masculine, feminine, or neuter—and the number—singular, dual, or plural—of that aforementioned [word]. This is the intended meaning: whatever [word] denotes a certain object is itself endowed with the gender and number of that very object. For example: *kārakaḥ puruṣaḥ* (the agent is a man), *kārikā strī* (the agent is a woman), *kārakaṃ kulam* (the agent is a family); *vaiyākaraṇaḥ puruṣaḥ* (the grammarian is a man), *vaiyākaraṇī strī* (the grammarian is a woman), *vaiyākaraṇaṃ kulam* (the grammarian is a family); *kṛtapraṇāmaḥ puruṣaḥ* (the one who has performed a salutation is a man).

A woman who has performed a prostration; a family that has performed a prostration; two women who act as attendants (*kārike*); women who act as attendants (*kārikāḥ*); two men who act as agents (*kārakau*); men who act as agents (*kārakāḥ*); in a family that acts as an agent (*kārake*); families that act as agents (*kārakāṇi*). And so forth. In this manner, the rules governing gender and number should be understood for other words formed with *kṛt*, *taddhita*, and compound suffixes. However, a verbal suffix (*ākhyātika-pratyaya*) cannot take on the gender [of its object]; it adopts only the number of what has been expressed. For example: "The cook cooks the rice."

Two cooks cook rice; many cooks cook rice. A woman cooks rice; two women cook rice; many women cook rice. A family cooks rice; two families cook rice; many families cook rice. In the same way: "A mat is being made by Devadatta"; "Two mats are being made by Devadatta"; "Mats are being made by Devadatta. Thus it is everywhere.

In connection with *tvam*, *yuvām*, and *yūyam*, the second person (*madhyama-puruṣa*) occurs according to the rule "after *yuṣmad*, the second person. For example: *tvaṃ bhavasi* (you are), *yuvāṃ bhavathaḥ* (you two are), *yūyaṃ bhavatha* (you all are). Likewise: *tvaṃ hanyase devadattena* (you are struck by Devadatta), *yuvāṃ hanyethe devadattena* (you two are struck by Devadatta), *yūyaṃ hanyadhve devadattena* (you all are struck by Devadatta). This applies everywhere. However, in connection with *aham*, *āvām*, and *vayam*, the first person (*uttama-puruṣa*) occurs according to the rule "after *asmad*, the first person. For example: *ahaṃ bhavāmi* (I am).

"May we two be," "may we be. Likewise: "I am struck by Devadatta," "we two are struck by Devadatta," "we are struck by Devadatta. This applies everywhere. However, when a personal name (*nāman*) is employed, the first person is used; for example: "Devadatta is," "Devadatta and [another] are," "Devadattas are. Also: "Devadatta overcomes you," "Devadatta knows me," "Rice is being cooked by you."

"A mat is being made by me" (*kriyate kaṭo mayā*). [Similarly: "I am staying" (*sthīyate mayā*); "you are existing" (*bhūyase tvayā*). Thus, the rule regarding gender and number has been stated for all cases. However, this was merely illustrated in the first verse as a mere indication of the direction; it has also been stated elsewhere through verbal suffixes (*ākhyāta*), primary derivatives (*kṛt*), secondary derivatives (*taddhita*), and compounds (*samāsa*), and should be understood through reasoning. When the suffix is prescribed in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*), then nothing [specific] is expressed. In that case, the suffix denoting the abstract state occurs after roots that are intransitive (*akarmaka*).

It also occurs after transitive roots if the object is not intended to be expressed. Examples: *bhūyate devadattena* (it is being by Devadatta), *sthīyate yuvābhyām* (it is being stood by you two), *pacyate asmābhiḥ* (it is being cooked by us), *gamyate devadattena* (it is being gone by Devadatta), and so forth. "Bhāva" (the abstract state) is existence (*sattā*). Since existence is without number, when it is the expressed meaning, the default singular number applies, and it occurs only in the first person. However, in the usage of *kṛt*-suffixes prescribed for the abstract state (*bhāva*), the factor of the object (*karma-kāraka*) must also be intended to be expressed.

The usage [of the accusative] is justified by the rule that even when a state (*bhāva*) is involved, there is a pervasion (*vyāpti*) established by the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), as in: "he is intent on going to the village" (*grāmaṃ gantuṃ udyataḥ*) or "having eaten the rice, he goes" (*odanaṃ bhuktvā vrajati*). This should be inferred in other cases as well. Now, it might be argued: "If something is 'expressed' (*ukta*) due to its connection with the primary action (*pradhānakriyā*), and 'unexpressed' (*anukta*) due to its connection with subordinate actions (*guṇakriyā*), then everything of that nature would indeed be considered expressed. If this were so, then in the sentence *odanaḥ paktvā bhujyate* ("the rice, having been cooked, is eaten"), the nominative case alone would apply to *odanaḥ* because its meaning has already been expressed [by the gerund]. [Response: This is not so. Even though the rice is connected with the primary action [of eating], it is not expressed by that action; rather, it is expressed by the subordinate action [of cooking]. Therefore, since it remains unexpressed with respect to the primary action, the accusative case is indeed appropriate. Furthermore, the word *odana* is not merely a synonym for *bhakta* (boiled rice); rather, it denotes a specific type of boiled rice characterized by particular qualities such as color, taste, and so forth. Consequently, since the rice is not expressed by the primary action, the accusative case is used. Thus, the rule is established: the object of the action denoted by the verbal root is expressed by the accusative case. In that case, regarding the sentence "Someone cooks and another employs him," there is the rule *dhātośca hetoḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.26). From the verbal root *pac*, the suffix *ṇic* is applied in the sense of the agent (*kartari*) with the *parasmaipada* ending: *pācayatyodanaṃ devadattena yajñadattaḥ* ("Yajñadatta causes Devadatta to cook the rice"). Because the agenthood has already been expressed [by the suffix], the nominative case (*prathamā*) is used for Yajñadatta as the agent. Since the agenthood of Devadatta is not expressed [by the suffix], the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*) is used for Devadatta as the agent. However, when Yajñadatta, who is the employer of Devadatta, is himself employed by Viṣṇumitra and thus causes [Devadatta] to cook: *(Note: The text provided ends mid-sentence; the translation reflects the grammatical analysis up to this point.)*

Thus, by this rule, even after [the suffix] *ṇic*, there is again the non-application [of the agent marker]. Viṣṇumitra causes Devadatta and Yajñadatta to cook the rice (*pācayaty odanaṃ devadattena yajñadattena viṣṇumitraḥ*). Here, because Viṣṇumitra—the agent—is expressed as the primary factor, the nominative case (*prathamā*) is used; however, when it is not expressed, the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*) is used everywhere. [In the case of roots] such as *duh* (to milk), the secondary object (*gauṇa-karma*) [is expressed in the accusative].

"Of *duh* and so forth," etc. This is its meaning: a suffix produced in the sense of the object (*karman*) expresses only the secondary object (*gauṇa-karman*), not the primary one (*pradhāna*). This is because of the rule of expression (*abhidhāna*). [The roots] beginning with *duh* are: *duh*, *yāc*, *rudh*, *pracch*, *bhikṣ*, *viñ*, and that which is the cause of application (*upayoga-nimitta*) in the case of *brū*, *śās*, and *guṇa*; and that which is "unmentioned" (*akīrtita*) by the poet—this is the established usage (*ācarita*). Here, by the word "and" (*ca*), roots such as *ji* (to conquer) and others are also included.

The fourth [group] consists of those that mean "to conquer" (*ji*), "to ask" (*yāc*), "to churn" (*manth*), and also "to punish" (*daṇḍ*); by these, the twelve roots beginning with *duh* (to milk) are to be known as having great intellects. The cow is milked of its milk by the cowherd (*gaur payo duhyate gopālakena*). The Paurava is asked for a blanket by the boy (*pauravaḥ kambalaṃ yācyate baṭunā*). The cow is kept from the pen by the cowherd (*gaur vrajaṃ rudhyate gopālakena*). The student is asked the way by the traveler (*chātraḥ panthānaṃ pṛcchyate pathikena*). The Paurava is begged for a cow by the twice-born (*pauravo gāṃ bhikṣyate dvijena*). Fruits are gathered from the tree by the people (*vrkṣaḥ phalāny avacīyate lokaiḥ*). The disciple is told the Dharma by the teacher (*śiṣyo dharmaṃ ucyate upādhyāyena*).

The disciple is instructed in the scripture by the learned man; likewise, the village is fined a hundred [pieces] by the student. The Gargas are fined a hundred by the king. A householder is requested for a cow by the twice-born; the ocean was churned for nectar by the gods and asuras. Here, since the milk and so forth being utilized are the primary objects (*karma*), the cow and so forth, which are the cause of that [utilization], are secondary (*gauṇa*). Because they are secondary, the Atmanepada ending prescribed for the object is used; thus, when expressed, the first case (*prathamā*) is employed for the object, but when unexpressed, the second case (*dvitīyā*) is used.

"The primary object [is the locus] of roots such as *nī* (to lead) and *vah* (to carry). "In this case, is it the agent, the object, or something else? Regarding verbs meaning "to understand" (*budh*), as for example: the disciple understands; the teacher causes the disciple to understand the Dharma. Maitra sees Caitra. The teacher causes the disciple to recite the scripture.

Devadatta speaks kindly. Yajñadatta causes Devadatta to speak kindly. As with intransitive verbs: "The pot arises" (*utpadyate ghaṭaḥ*) [becomes] "The potter produces the pot" (*ghaṭam utpādayati kulālaḥ*). "The rice remains in the husk" (*kośam āste vrīhiḥ*) [becomes] "The farmer causes the rice to remain in the husk" (*kośam āsayati vrīhīn kṛṣīvalaḥ*). "Devadatta sleeps until the cooking of the rice is finished" (*udanapākam svapiti devadattaḥ*) [becomes] "Yajñadatta causes Devadatta to sleep until the cooking of the rice is finished" (*udanapākam svāpayati devadattaṃ yajñadattaḥ*).

In this manner, the object (*karman*) of all roots meaning "motion" (*gatyartha*) and the like should be understood everywhere. However, when roots meaning motion and the like ending in *ṇic* are intended to express another causal factor (*aparahetu*), then [the following] should be inferred: "Viṣṇumitra causes Devadatta to go to the village by means of Yajñadatta" (*grāmam gamayati devadattam yajñadattena viṣṇumitraḥ*). But in the case of the object, it is: "Devadatta is made to go to the village by Yajñadatta and Viṣṇumitra" (*grāmam gamyate devadatto yajñadattena viṣṇumitreṇa*), and so forth.

Or rather, when these two [roots] have the sense of "begging for alms" (*bhikṣārthatva*), there is a prohibition regarding their [being used with an instrumental]. The application [of the rule] is as follows: *bhakṣayati piṇḍīṃ devadattena yajñadattaḥ* ("Yajñadatta causes Devadatta to eat the cake"). Devadatta causes the porter to carry the load to the village; this is indeed an operation whose agent is the charioteer (sārathikartṛka). Or, for example: "The charioteer causes the oxen to carry the grain to the village. Other [roots] are treated similarly.
Likewise, with the roots *hṛ* ("to take") and *kṛ* ("to do"), the agent may likewise become the object when the suffix *ṇic* is added.

Regarding the rule *hr̥kror* and so forth: "likewise" (*tathā*) means by the intention to express pervasion (*vyāpya-vivakṣayā*). Since the roots *hr̥* (to carry) and *dṛś* (to see) have the meanings of motion and cognition respectively, they would [otherwise] require the option (*vibhāṣā*) [of the *saṇic* affix]. For the root *kr̥*, the option is already established because it has the sense of "honoring" (*abhivādyo'sya*). The examples are: *hārayati bhāraṃ grāmaṃ devadattaṃ yajñadattaḥ* ("Yajñadatta causes Devadatta to carry the load to the village")—or alternatively, *devadattena*. *kārayati kaṭaṃ devadattaṃ yajñadattaḥ* ("Yajñadatta causes Devadatta to make a mat")—or alternatively, *devadattena*.
In the case of the roots *abhivadi* (to greet) and *dṛś* (to see), when used in the middle voice (*ātmanepada*), the same applies to the other [object]. (9)

Regarding the rule *abhivādidṛśoḥ*: the term *abhivādī* is derived from the root *vad* with the suffix *ghañ*, followed by the addition of the suffix *in* according to the *cūrtādi* group, and subsequently the causal suffix *ṇic*. Thus, it means "one who causes [another] to salute. Examples include: *janakaḥ tanayam gurum abhivādayate* (The father causes the son to salute the teacher). Or, according to the rule *tena yena vā* (Pāṇini 1.4.33), one may say: *rājā bhṛtyam ātmānam darśayate* (The king shows himself to the servant) or *bhṛtyena* (through the servant). This restriction—that the rule *abhivādidṛśoḥ* applies only within the domain of the Ātmanepada—is established because, in the domain of the Parasmaipada, the operation occurs exactly as prescribed by the general rules. For example: *lokaḥ bhṛtyena svāminam abhivādayati* (The person causes the master to be saluted by the servant). In this case, there is simply an intention to express the agent (*kartṛvivakṣā*).

Viṣṇumitra shows Maitra Caitra. Since the root *dṛś* (to see) has the sense of cognition (*bodha*), it takes the object (*karman*) case. Regarding the rule "the agent of roots other than those ending in *gatyartha* up to *dṛś*, when followed by *aniṇ* [causative suffixes]," this [agent] also remains an agent and does not become an object. For example: Yajñadatta causes Devadatta to cook the rice; Viṣṇumitra causes Caitra to give the cow; Devadatta causes the cowherd to milk the cow for milk—and so on with others.
Everywhere, according to the same principle established previously, the causal agent (*hetu*) is indeed the agent (*kartṛ*).
That which has not been stated would be "unexpressed" (*anukta*); however, that which has been stated is indeed [the domain of] the first case alone.

Because the unexpressed is established based on what has been expressed, the introduction of the case-endings (*vibhakti*) follows immediately after. Regarding the rule "in the expressed, there is indeed the first case alone": here the word *eva* (indeed) serves for restriction. When a factor (*kāraka*) or a relation (*saṃbandha*) has been expressed, only the first case-ending occurs. This is because of the statement: "The first case-ending is used for the meaning of gender (*liṅga*). No other [case], such as the second and so forth, occurs, because they have already been expressed. This is according to the rule: "There is no employment of words whose meaning has already been expressed. The intention is this: the second case is prescribed for the purpose of expressing "object" (*karman*) and so forth.

But where the expression of [grammatical categories] such as "object-ness" (*karmatva*) has been performed by others, how do the second case endings (*dvitīyā*) and so forth occur there? For example: *devadatto bhavati* (Devadatta exists); *kaṭaḥ kriyate* (the mat is being made); *snānīyaṃ varṇam* (color for bathing); *dānīyo brāhmaṇaḥ* (a Brāhmaṇa worthy of a gift); *utsannajanapado deśaḥ* (a country whose inhabitants have perished); *āsanaṃ pīṭham* (a seat, a stool); *gomān devadattaḥ* (Devadatta possesses cows). Other examples should be understood in the same way. Having explained the case endings already mentioned, he now speaks to explain those not yet mentioned by means of the general category of case endings:
"But when [the relation] is unexpressed, the other [case endings], beginning with the second, occur according to their respective rules. (10)

Regarding the phrase "anukte tu" (but when [the case] is not stated), etc.: when [the case] is not stated, with the exception of the nominative (*prathamā*), the other cases beginning with the accusative (*dvitīyā*) occur according to their respective requirements. Whichever case among the accusative and so forth is prescribed for a particular meaning occurs in that context. The meaning of "yathāyatham" (according to what is appropriate) is limited. Therefore, starting from this point, the rule regarding the cases (*vibhakti-niyama*) which was indicated by the term "yathāyatham" is now set forth: "The third case (*tṛtīyā*) shall occur when [the agent] has the designation 'agent' (*kartṛ-saṃjñā*)."

The third case ending occurs for the *kāraka* designated as the agent (*kartṛ*). This is because of the rule stating "and when [the agent] is expressed. That which functions primarily toward the accomplishment of an action—that is, which performs or brings about the action—receives the designation of agent (*kartṛ*). For example: "Devadatta cooks rice in a pot with firewood. Here, Devadatta is the agent; for it is by Devadatta that the collection of factors is impelled to bring about the action through its own respective operations, such as burning.
