Devadatta alone possesses effort; therefore, he alone is the primary agent (*kartṛ*), and not other things such as wood and so forth. Thus, in all cases, he is twofold: both independent (*svatantra*) and a cause (*hetu*). In that regard, the instigator (*prayojaka*) of the aforementioned type—such as Devadatta and others—is the independent one who acts; such a cause is designated by the technical term "agent" (*kartṛ-saṃjñā*). And that [cause] is of three kinds: the instigating cause (*preṣaka-hetu*), which is like the moon; or the one who partakes in favorability (*ānukūlyabhāgī*).

In this context, he who sends forth—that is, appoints by virtue of his authority—is the sender (*preṣaka*). Here, for example, Devadatta, as the master, appoints a servant with a command to make a mat. Furthermore, he who requests—that is, appoints preceded by honor—is the requester (*adhyeṣaka*). For example, in the case of "Yajñadatta feeds the teacher," Yajñadatta appoints the teacher preceded by honor.

Furthermore, that which adopts a state of favorability toward the performance of an action by the object to be employed—neither commanding nor entreating—is a participant in favorability (*ānukūlyabhāgī*). That [participant] is of two kinds: sentient (*sacetana*) and insentient (*acetana*). Among these, the sentient is as follows: "The good son gladdens his father. In this case, the good son, while indeed adopting a state of favorability toward the father's gladdening, thus enjoins him to it.

However, an insentient entity, while acting as an instigator (*prayojaka*), is merely one who partakes in conformity (*ānukūlyabhāgī*); it is neither a commander (*preṣaka*) nor an entreator (*adhyeṣaka*). This is because an insentient thing is incapable of performing the acts of commanding or entreating. Just as in the expression "the fire of dried cow-dung (*kārīṣo'gniḥ*) teaches the boy," here the fire of dried cow-dung, by burning and removing cold and other such obstacles, partakes in conformity with the act of studying and thereby instigates him. In this case, the third case-ending (*tṛtīyā*) should be used for the designation of the agent (*kartṛsaṃjñā*).

In this context, "causative agency" (*prayojakatva*) refers to that which causes another to act; thus, such a person receives both the designation of "cause" (*hetu*) and the designation of "agent" (*kartṛ*). When an agent of this kind is not explicitly mentioned, the third case (*tṛtīyā*) is to be understood. Examples: *devadattena kriyate kaṭaḥ* ("A mat is being made by Devadatta"); *yajñadattena kāryate bhṛtyena kaṭaḥ* ("A mat is caused to be made by Yajñadatta through a servant"); *viṣṇumitreṇa bhojyate odanaṃ guruḥ* ("The teacher is fed rice by Viṣṇumitra"); *suputreṇa modyate janakaḥ* ("The father is gladdened by his good son"); *kārīṣeṇādhmayate māṇavakaḥ* ("The boy is made to blow with dried cow-dung"). Likewise: *tvayā kṛtam* ("It was done by you"); *mayoktam* ("It was said by me"). Other examples are to be understood similarly. The second case (*dvitīyā*) is used for the object (*karman*) kāraka.

The connection is that "the second [case-ending] shall occur when there is the factor of the object (*karmakāraka*). This is because of the statement, "The remainder [are the agent, etc.]," and "that which is acted upon by the agent is the object. That *kāraka* which is acted upon by the agent's action—that which is pervaded, or that which has the pervasion of the agent's action—is designated as the object (*karman*). And that is of three kinds: the produced (*nirvartya*), the modified (*vikārya*), and the reached (*prāpya*). Among these, that which is brought into being, accomplished, or produced while previously non-existent is the produced (*nirvartya*).

For example, a potter makes a jar. In this case, the jar—which was previously non-existent—is produced from clay. Therefore, regarding the nature of the jar, the "attainment" (prāpti) of its mere birth through the potter’s act of making is called *anulambha*. That which undergoes transformation (*vikriyate*) by being made otherwise than it was is the "transformable" (*vikārya*). For example, Devadatta burns wood.

In this context, wood is indeed that which is transformed by burning; therefore, the transformation (*vikāra*) here—namely, the alteration of the wood through the agent Devadatta’s act of burning—is called "attainment" (*prāpti*). That [transformation] is also of two kinds: first, that which consists in the non-destruction of the material cause (*prakṛti*), as previously described; the other is by way of the imposition of superior qualities (*guṇottarādhāna*). An example of the latter, involving a change of designation (*vyapadeśāntara*), is: "He makes gold into an earring. For here, by means of the designation "earring," the manifestation of the gold is established.

The same should be understood in cases such as "he whitens the temple" (*devakulaṃ dhavalayati*). That which is not produced anew (*apūrva*) nor transformed otherwise, but rather always exists and is made the object through the act of apprehension (*viṣayīkriyā*), being connected as an object—this very connection of the Veda is here called "attainment" (*prāpti*). When an action (*karman*) of this kind is unexpressed, then the accusative case (*dvitīyā*) is to be understood. For example: *kuṃbhaṃ karoti kuṃbhakāraḥ* ("the potter makes a pot").

Devadatta burns wood; the Brahmin studies the Veda. Likewise: Devadatta has made a mat. The cowherd goes to milk the cow. Thus it is everywhere. Regarding the rule: "Then the sixth case (genitive) occurs for those two [agent and object], except when used with kṛt suffixes such as the niṣṭhā. For those two—the agent and the object—when not already expressed, the genitive occurs upon the employment of a kṛt suffix other than the niṣṭhā, because of the statement: "The genitive is obligatory for the agent and the object when a kṛt suffix follows."

However, when used with past passive participles (*niṣṭhā*) and the like, the third case (*tṛtīyā*) is employed for the agent and the second case (*dvitīyā*) for the object. This is because of the prohibition of the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) by the rule *na niṣṭhādiṣu*. For example, regarding the agent: *bhavata āsikā* (the sitting of your honor), *bhavataḥ śāyikā* (the lying down of your honor). Also [the rule applies] in the case of synonyms for "taking turns" (*paryāya*) and "bringing" (*āharaṇa*).

When the suffix *buñ* is used in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*), the agent is not expressed; however, when it is used in the sense of an object (*karman*), the agent is expressed as in "Devadatta is the cooker of rice" (*udanasya pācako devadattaḥ*) or "having cooked" (*paktvā*). Or, as in "Hara is the shatterer of the cities" (*purāṃbhedako haraḥ*) or "the breaker" (*bhettā*). But in the case of verbs with multiple objects, as long as the object remains unexpressed, the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) occurs for that unexpressed object—not only for the primary object, since there is no distinction [in the rule]. For example: "the milker of cows" (*gavāṃ dohakaḥ*) or "the cowherd of milk" (*payaso gopālakaḥ*), or "the milker" (*dogdhā*); or "Devadatta is the leader of the village by means of the goats" (*ajāyā grāmasya nāyako devadattaḥ*) or "the guide" (*netā*).

Yajñadatta is the one who causes Devadatta to go to the village, or he is the one who causes him to go. Devadatta is the one who causes Maitra to sit for a month, or he is the one who causes him to sit. In this way, the genitive case occurs everywhere in the context of verbs governing two objects; even where there are three objects, the genitive occurs in all such instances. For example: Yajñadatta is the one who causes Vaṇṭha to carry the load of the jar, or he is the one who causes him to carry it. Similarly, Maitra is the one who causes the teacher to recite the Dharma to the pupil, or he is the one who causes him to recite it.

In the case of the root *brū* (to speak), the agent who is prompted [to act] is treated as the object (*karman*). This applies everywhere in such cases. Since the suffixes *vuṇ* and *tṛc* are prescribed for the agent (*kartṛ*), the object remains unexpressed (*anukta*). Here, it is stated that even when a *kṛt* suffix is used with a verb meaning "motion" (*gatyartha*), the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) does not occur; rather, according to some, the dative case (*caturthī*) occurs for the object of a motion-verb. According to that view, the explicit mention of the accusative (*dvitīyā*) in the rule indicates an effort [to exclude the dative]. Thus: *grāmaṃ gantā devadattaḥ* or *grāmāya gantā devadattaḥ*.

Thus, one finds such forms as *devadattasya yajñadattaḥ grāmaṃ gamayitā* (Yajñadatta is the one who causes Devadatta to go to the village) or *grāmāya* (or [to] the village). However, this is not approved by the author of the commentary (*ṭīkākāra*), nor are such usages seen among the learned (*śiṣṭa*). Therefore, for this reason, we have simply disregarded this position. Now, regarding the specific grammatical derivation (*prakriyā*) in examples such as *udanasya bhṛśaṃ pācakaḥ* (one who cooks rice thoroughly), why is there no genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) when the object (*karman*) is a qualifier? True; [the form] is *udanasya pācakaḥ*. [Objection: In the case of *kaṭaṃ karoti* (he makes a mat), why does the genitive not occur after *kaṭa*?

Now, if it is argued that the object of the verb *karoti* (he makes) is the mat (*kaṭa*), but not that of the agent *pācaka* (the cooker), because the genitive case is prescribed after a root ending in a *kṛt*-suffix when the object is expressed—how then could the genitive arise from *kaṭāt*? If this is so, then the same applies even to an adverbial adjunct (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*), since every meaning of a verbal root is pervaded by the sense of "doing" (*karoti*). Thus, the status of being an object for an adverbial adjunct would occur only through the mediation of the action of "doing," and yet such is not the case.

In the expression *māsasyāsakaḥ* ("one who sits for a month"), since the action of reaching (*prāpaṇa*) is understood [as inherent], the month is the object (*karman*) of that action; thus, the genitive case does not apply. This is because verbs such as *ās-* ("to sit") and others denote actions like sitting which have the action of "reaching" (*prāpti*) included within them. According to the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), the month is the object of the very action of sitting itself. Therefore, it is sufficient to say that there is no need for further discussion regarding an implied action distinct from that primary action. The phrase "excluding the past participles (*niṣṭhā*) and so forth" refers to the following: the past participles (*niṣṭhā*) are the suffixes *kta*, *ktavatu*, *śatṛ*, and *śānac*; the suffixes *āna* and *thaN*; and those ending in *suK* and *ud*.

The suffixes *ukañ*, *tṛn*, and those having the sense of the *avyaya* and *khalartha* [are used]. Among these, the example for the *kta* suffix is as follows: *gato grāmaṃ devadattaḥ* (Devadatta went to the village); *gato grāmo devadattena* (the village was gone to by Devadatta). By the rule beginning with *gatyarthākarmaka-* etc., the *kta* suffix is applied to both the agent (*kartṛ*) and the object (*karman*). Similarly: *payogau dugdhā devadattena* (two milks were milked by Devadatta); *odanaḥ pakvaḥ devadattena* (rice was cooked by Devadatta); *yajñadattena* (by Yajñadatta). By the rule beginning with *bhāvakarmaṇoḥ* etc., the *kta* suffix is applied in the sense of the object (*karman*). Regarding the statement *kartari kṛt* ("the *kṛt* suffix occurs in the sense of the agent"): this suffix occurs in the sense of the agent because of the mention of the term *niṣṭhā*.

In all cases, the suffixes *kta*, *ktavat*, *śatṛ*, and *ānaś* [are used]. For example: *udanaṃ pacan sūpakārastiṣṭhati* (the cook stands cooking rice); *grāmamajāṃ nayan yajñadattaḥ kliśyati* (Yajñadatta suffers while leading the goat to the village). Regarding the present tense, by the rule *śatṛ-ānaśāvityādinā*, the suffixes *śatṛ* and *ānaś* are used in the sense of the agent (*kartari*). However, it is not only in the sense of the agent; for there is the statement *āno'trātmane* [indicating they are also used in the reflexive voice]. They also occur in the sense of the action (*bhāve*) and the object (*karmaṇi*), according to the statement *evaṃ kvaṃsukānauparokṣāvatvaiti*. Thus, there are *kvaṃs* and *kāna*; *kvaṃs* is used in the sense of the agent.

The suffix *kāna* occurs in all three voices (*padas*). In the rule "āne kāna-ānaś-ānaḍāṃ" (*Pāṇini 6.4.69*), there is a selection of those [suffixes] having the most prominent indicatory letter (*anubandha*). Among them, for *kāna*, as an example in the active voice (*kartari*): *kaṭaṃ cakāṇo devadattaḥ* ("Devadatta has made a mat"); *payogāṃ duduhāno gopālakaḥ* ("the cowherd is milking the cows"). As an example in the passive voice (*karmaṇi*): *kaṭaścakāṇo devadattena* ("a mat was made by Devadatta"); *payogaurduduhano gopālakena* ("the cow was milked by the cowherd"). For *ānaś*, as an example in the active voice: *odanaṃ pacamāno gāyati sūpakāraḥ* ("the cook, while cooking rice, sings"); *grāmamajāṃ nayamānaḥ puruṣaḥ kliśyati* ("the man leading the goat to the village suffers"). As an example in the passive voice: [omitted in source].

Rice is prepared while being cooked by the cook; a goat does not run away when being led to the village—thus [the suffix] *śānac* is used in the sense of the object (*karman*). As for *śānac*: "How many here are slaying their enemies, wearing armor, the Kṣatriya princes? "How many here are licking honey, desiring wealth? Since the suffix *śānac* is prescribed after verbal roots expressing "habitual action" (*tācchīlya*), it occurs only in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*). Regarding the mention of *kvaṃsu* and *vaṃsu*: the inclusion of *kvaṃsu* and *vaṃsu* is as follows: *kvaṃsu*, for example, [is seen in the phrase] *suvam*.

The suffix *vaṃsu* occurs only when the agent (*kartṛ*) is expressed, as in: "the cook who has cooked the broth" (*udanaṃ pecivān sūpakāraḥ*), "the cowherd who has milked the cows" (*gopayo duduhvān gopālakaḥ*). For example: "Devadatta who has made a mat" (*kaṭaṃ citvān devadattaḥ*). According to the rule *vetteḥ śatur vaṃsuḥ*, the suffix *vaṃsu* is the substitute for the suffix *śatṛ*. Examples of its occurrence with the feminine gender (*strīliṅga*) are: "Devadatta who has made a mat" (*kaṭaṃ cakrī devadattaḥ*) and "Devadatta who has fashioned a jar" (*dadhiṣvī ghaṭaṃ devadattaḥ*).

The suffix *kip* occurs after roots ending in *ṛ*, as in the example *āṭṭ* (from the root *aṭ*), according to the rule "after roots ending in *ṛ*, *kip* is applied when the sense is that of the agent" (*nāṃkiddhai ceti vacanāt*). There is also reduplication. By the rule "ending in *ud*" (*udaṃteti*), there is the inclusion of all *kṛt* suffixes ending in the vowel *u*. For example: "the father who desires to adorn his daughter" (*kanyāmalaṃkariṣṇuḥ pitā*); "Yajñadatta who causes Devadatta to go to the village" (*grāmaṃ gamayiṣṇur devadattaṃ yajñadattaḥ*). By the rule beginning with "after *bhrāj*, *alaṃkṛ*, *bhū*, *sah*, etc. (*bhrājyalaṃkṛñbhūsahi ityādinā*), the suffix *iṣṇu* is also applied in the sense of the agent alone, denoting habit, duty, or proficiency (*taśīlataddharmatatsādhukāriṣu*). Similarly: "the weaver who wishes to make a cloth" (*paṭaṃ cikīrṣustaṃtuvāyaḥ*).

A *paiṇḍapātika* (alms-seeker) is one who desires (*bubhukṣu*) rice. Regarding suffixes such as *san*, *āśaṃsin*, and *bhikṣu*, the suffix *ukañ* is used only in the sense of the agent (*kartari*), as in: "a bridegroom desirous of a maiden" (*kanyā-kāmukaḥ*) or "a person going to a village" (*grāma-gāmukaḥ*). Regarding suffixes such as *śruka*, *gamaka*, and so forth, the suffix *ukañ* is used only in the sense of the agent, as in: "those who have gone among all-knowers" (*sarvajñātāsu gataḥ*) or "shaving priests" (*muṇḍayitāraḥ*). [The term] *śrāviṣṭāyinaḥ* refers to those who, due to public scandal, have been deceived regarding their wives (*vadhū-mūrdha-viditāḥ*); here the suffix *tṛn* is used only in the sense of the agent. [Regarding the rule] "avyaya": this is a reference to indeclinables that function as *kṛt* suffixes.

It has been stated that the suffix *ktvā* and that which ends in *m* are indeclinables (*avyaya*) because they possess the nature of *kṛt* suffixes and are not [part of] a number. Likewise, the employment of the *kṛt* suffix *ktvā* ending in *m* occurs in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāva*). This is certain. In this regard, an example of *ktvā* is as follows: "Having gone to the village, Devadatta eats" (*grāmaṃ gatvā devadatto bhuṅkte*); "Having milked the cow, the cowherd sells [the milk]" (*gāṃ payo dugdhvā gopālako vikrīṇīte*); and "Having bowed to you, the kinsman departed" (*evaṃ bhavantaṃ praṇamya svajano gataḥ*). By the rule "when there is a single agent, [the suffix] *ktvā* is used for the prior time," the suffix *ktvā* is applied; and by the rule "in a compound, *ya* is substituted for *a*" (*samāse bhāvinītyādinā*), the substitution of *ya* for *a* occurs.

Examples of forms ending in *m*: "Devadatta stands in order to make a mat" (*kaṭaṃ kartuṃ devadattastiṣṭhati*); "People begin to lead the goat to the village" (*grāmamajāṃ netumupakramet lokaḥ*). In these cases, the suffix *tum* is used according to the rule *tumunṇvulau kriyāyāṃ kriyārthāyām*. Likewise: "In this world, states of being perish like bubbles on water; prosperity is but momentary. In that context, regarding how prosperity perishes, the suffix *ṇamul* is used according to the rule *bhūṣākṛñprāpti... vābhīkṣṇye dve ca padasya*, followed by reduplication. By the rule *khalarthāḥ*, both the suffix *khal* and the suffix *yus* are included.

In that regard, it is as follows: The word *khal* is used in the senses of "slight," "difficulty," "pain," and "hardship. For example: "Easy for you was the wood; wealth is difficult to obtain by those lacking resolve; the end of calamity is easily reached by the wise; the destruction of enemies is easily achieved by the courageous. The suffix *yu* is used as follows: "Soma is indeed slightly drunk by the initiated; the forest is difficult to traverse by a villager; wealth is easily given by a lord. Here, the suffix *yu* is applied after the root *dā* (to give) following the prefix *su-*. Similarly: "Difficult to govern is the enemy situated in a fortress by a king; or rather, he is one who is difficult to be commanded."

The suffix *yu* occurs optionally after the roots *śās*, *yudh*, *dṛś*, and the roots ending in *ṛṣ*, according to the rule "vā vikalpena yuḥ. Elsewhere, the suffix *yu* is treated as before; this very suffix *yu* is shown in the sense of the *khala* suffixes. It should be understood that it applies to the agent (*bhava*) and the object (*karman*), and not merely that which is prescribed by [the rule] beginning with "su-duḥ-dvi-. Thus, other examples of these should also be understood exactly according to the sūtras. In this way, because the *kṛtya* suffixes are accepted in the alternative case among the *niṣṭhā* suffixes and others, the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) optionally occurs for the agent. For example: [Example omitted per instructions.]

"Devadatta’s mat is to be made," "is to be done," "is to be performed," or "is to be accomplished. [In these cases,] it is by Devadatta. The suffixes *tavya* and *anīya* [are used] after a word ending in a vowel or a consonant; the suffix *kyap* is used optionally after roots such as *kṛ*, *dṛś*, and *mṛṣ*. Thus, in all cases, even for actions involving multiple agents, the genitive case is optionally employed for the agent up to this point. For example: "Rice is to be caused to be cooked for Devadatta by Yajñadatta"—[this may be expressed as] "by Devadatta" or "by Yajñadatta. The same applies in both instances (the passive and the causative). For instance: *devadattasya kaṭaḥ kartavyaḥ | kāryaḥ | karaṇīyaḥ | kṛtyo vā | devadatteneti |* *tavyānīyau varṇavyañjanāntād dhy-aṇ |* *kṛdṛṣimṛṣāṃ veti kyap |* *evaṃ sarvatrānekakartṛkāṇām api yāvat kartari vikalpena ṣaṣṭhī bhavati |* *pācayitavya odano devadattāya yajñadattasya devadattena yajñadattena vā |* *evam indvaye 'pi |* *tad yathā |* The mat of Devadatta is to be made, is to be done, is to be performed, or is to be accomplished—by Devadatta. The suffixes *tavya* and *anīya* occur after words ending in vowels or consonants; the suffix *kyap* occurs optionally after the roots *kṛ*, *dṛś*, and *mṛṣ*. Thus, in all cases, even for those [actions] having multiple agents, the genitive is optionally used for the agent up to this point. Rice is to be caused to be cooked for Devadatta by Yajñadatta—[expressed as] "for Devadatta" or "by Yajñadatta. The same applies in both cases. For example:

"Rice is to be cooked for Devadatta, Yajñadatta, or Viṣṇumitra," or "by Devadatta, by Yajñadatta, or by Viṣṇumitra"—thus it is in all cases. But how is it that in expressions such as *rājñāṃ mātā devadattaḥ* ("Devadatta is the mother of the kings"), the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) occurs in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*) when the suffix *kta* is employed according to the rule beginning with *ñyanubandha*? Is it not true that *kta* is also admitted among the *niṣṭhā* suffixes? True; here the genitive is used because the relationship of the agent is intended to be expressed.

Likewise, in the case of the *kta* suffix used in the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇe*), when there is a connection with a *kta* suffix prescribed for a locus by the rule "after roots meaning steadiness, motion, or eating" (*dhrauvyagatipratyavasānārthebhyaḥ*), the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is to be understood in relation to the agent (*kartṛ*). For example: "The village where Devadatta used to stay is occupied by Devadatta" (*tiṣṭhati sma grāme yasmin devadattaḥ sa sthito grāmo devadattasya*). Similarly: "The village reached by Devadatta" (*gato grāmo devadattasya*); "Viṣṇumitra’s brass vessel eaten" (*bhuktaṃ kāṃsyabhājanaṃ viṣṇumitrasya*). The same applies to other instances as well.

Thus, when the *kta* suffix is prescribed in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāva*), the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) occurs either in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*) or in the sense of a relationship (*saṃbandha*). For example: *tvayā kṛtam* ("done by you") or *(mayā kṛtam)* ("done by me"). This applies everywhere; furthermore, the *kta* suffix is used in the neuter gender for the abstract action (*bhāve*). However, there is this distinction: it will be summarized by the verse beginning with *prāyaḥ sahoktau kavitā eva*, etc.
But when both [the agent and the object] are eligible [to take the sixth case], it is used only for the object (*karman*), not for the agent (*kartṛ*).

"Ekadā tu," and so forth. At one time, however, when there is the possibility of the genitive case applying to both [the agent and the object], the genitive occurs only for the object (*karman*), not for the agent (*kartṛ*). But when the suffix *akā* is not employed, the genitive would apply to both. "At one time" (*ekadā*) means at one point in time, that is to say, in a construction involving a *kṛt* suffix. When there is the possibility of the genitive applying to both the agent and the object, the genitive occurs only for the object and not for the agent. That "possibility of application to both" refers to a usage where both the agent and the object remain unexpressed. Example: *pācayitā bhaktasya devadattena yajñadattaḥ* ("Yajñadatta is the one who causes Devadatta to cook the rice").

Or [the agent is] the cooker (*pācaka*). Or the leader (*nāyaka*), such as the master who causes the village or the burden to be led by a servant. Thus, in both these cases—for example: Viṣṇumitra causes Devadatta to cook rice by means of Yajñadatta; or he is the cooker (*pācaka*). Or: Viṣṇumitra causes Devadatta to go to the village by means of Yajñadatta; or he is the goer (*gamaka*). In such instances involving transitive verbs with multiple agents, the suffix prescribed for the agent expresses only the primary agent. This is called "the attainment of both" (*ubhayaprāpti*).

Therefore, the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) occurs [for the agent] as long as it is not expressed; likewise, the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*) occurs for the agent when it is not expressed. For example: *dogdhavyā gauḥ payasaḥ gopālakena* ("The cow is to be milked of its milk by the cowherd"); *netavyo bhāraḥ grāmasya vaṃṭhena* ("The load is to be carried to the village by the porter"). Similarly: *gamayitavyo 'dhyāpakaḥ śiṣyasya dharmasya caitreṇa* ("The teacher is to be made to go by Caitra for the sake of the student's dharma"), and *nāyayitavyo bhāraḥ grāmasya vaṃṭhena* ("The load is to be caused to be carried to the village by the porter"). O Master! This applies even in the case of roots meaning "to go" (*gatyartha*), whether the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is present or not: *gamayitavyo devadatto grāmasya yajñadattena viṣṇumitreṇa*, etc.

In such cases as these, where a suffix prescribed for the object is applied to both the agent and the object of roots like *duh* (to milk), it expresses only one object, based on the rule stating that "for roots beginning with *duh*, the object is secondary. Therefore, when both [agent and object] are eligible for the genitive, the genitive occurs only for the object so long as it is not already expressed by another case; however, for the agent, the instrumental alone is used everywhere. Consequently, some say that because of the rule "for gerundives (*kṛtya*), [the genitive] optionally for the agent," the [genitive] does not apply to the agent in the case of roots having multiple objects. We, however, say: "(When both are eligible, the genitive does not occur for the object in the case of gerundives)."

And thus, there occurs only such [examples] as "the cow whose milk has been milked by the cowherd" (*dogdhavayā gauḥ payo gopālakena*) or "the load must be carried to the village by the porter" (*netavyo bhāro grāmaṃ vaṃṭhena*), and so forth; however, the detailed expansion of examples shown previously does not apply. This being the case, both of these explanations are justified for the rule *uvarme stautyamāpadya* (Pāṇini 1.4.29), which states that the suffix *kṛtya* is applied after a root ending in *u* when the agent is not the object (*amāpadya*). Furthermore, Jayāditya also demonstrates this very point in the rule *kṛtyānāṃ kartari vā* (Pāṇini 3.4.71). For example:

When both [the agent and the object] are applicable, a prohibition of the genitive case must be stated for the *kṛtya* suffixes. Thus it is established: *vāḍhavyā grāmaṃ śākhā devadattena* ("The branch is to be carried to the village by Devadatta") and *netavyā grāmam ajā devadattena* ("The goat is to be led to the village by Devadatta"). This also applies to abstract nominal suffixes (*bhāvapratyaya*) of transitive verbs; because of the rule "when both are applicable," as long as the genitive is used for the object, the instrumental remains for the agent. Examples: *udanasya pāko devadattena* ("The cooking of water by Devadatta") or *pacanaṃ devadattena*; *gavāṃ dohaḥ payaso gopālakena* ("The milking of cows/milk by the cowherd") or *dohanaṃ gopālakena*.

The leading of a village or a load by a porter (*vaṃṭha*). [Note: *naya* is derived from the root *nī* with the suffix *ghañ* in the sense of an action, according to the rule *śriṇībhūbhyo upasarge*]. The cooking of rice by Devadatta and Yajñadatta. The going to the village by Caitra and Viṣṇumitra. The leading of a load or a village by a porter or a master. Even in the case of two agents: the cooking of rice by Devadatta, Yajñadatta, and Viṣṇumitra; the going to the village by Caitra and Viṣṇumitra—such examples are to be inferred.

In all instances where there is a sense of "being" (*bhāva*), the suffixes *ghañ* and *yuṭ* apply; thus, for roots such as *kṛñ* ending in *i*, the forms are easily understood under both alternatives. For example: *bhārasya hāraḥ* (the carrying of a burden), *grāmasya hāraḥ* by Devadatta, or *hāraṇam* by Yajñadatta. Now, one might ask: how can there be a genitive case for the agent in the expression *āścaryo gavāṃ payaso doho gopālakasya* ("It is a wonder, the milking of the cows' milk by the cowherd")? True; when the relationship of the agent is intended to be expressed, the genitive is used, so there is no fault. Furthermore, the form *āścaryo gavāṃ payaso doho gopālakena* (with the instrumental) also occurs in the sense of the agent.

Since the rule "the [genitive] is used for the agent and the object when a word ending in a *kṛt* suffix follows" (Pāṇini 2.3.65) is already established by the rule "the [genitive] is used for the object of a verb whose meaning is 'remembering'" (Pāṇini 2.3.52), the repetition of the word "object" (*karman*) in the former rule is stated for the purpose of restricting it to the object alone when both [agent and object] are possible. Thus, when both are possible, the restriction would result in the genitive being used for the object alone; in response to this, he states a specific exception:
"But when there is the employment of a suffix with the augment *aK* or *āK*, the genitive should be used for both. (Verse 12)

However, in the case of a suffix beginning with *a* (aka), the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) should apply to both [the agent and the object]. The mention of *aka* here refers to the suffix *buñ*, because [the suffix] *ka* is included within the rule *yu-buñ-ādayaḥ*. The mention of *akāra* refers to the suffixes *aṇ* and *ḍa*; when these are employed, the genitive occurs for both the agent and the object. For example, with a suffix beginning with *a*: *pācikā bhaktasya devadattasya* ("the cook of Devadatta's food") and *gavāṃ dohikā payaso gopālakasya* ("the milker of the cows' milk by the cowherd"). Thus, in all such cases, the genitive must be applied to both the agent and the object. Enough of this elaboration.

In the rule *paryāyāharaṇeṣu vā*, because of the statement "it is seen even in the case of mere action (*bhāvamātra*)," the suffix *vuñ* occurs even for mere action. For example: *cikīrṣā kaṭasya devadattasya* (Devadatta’s desire to make a mat), *jihīrṣā bhārasya grāmasya vaṇṭhasya* (the village headman’s desire to take away the load). Likewise, with the two forms of the causative suffix (*ṇic*), we have *pācayitā bhaktasya sūpakārasya devadattasya* (Devadatta the cook’s role as the one who causes the food to be cooked). Similarly, with the desiderative suffix (*san*), we have *pipāciṣā bhaktasya devadattasya yajñadattasya viṣṇumitrasya* (Devadatta, Yajñadatta, and Viṣṇumitra’s desire to cause the food to be cooked). In all these instances, the genitive case is used; however, in the usage *mālāyāḥ saṃskartā*, the genitive is used [not because of the action, but] because of the suffix *saṃs* (from *saṃskaroti*). Thus it is not uniform.

The suffix *ṣa* (ṅīṣ) occurs after words ending in *udana*, *pacā*, feminine nouns, and after *bhida*, *kārin*, *kuṃbha*, and *kesarin*. The scope of this rule is easily understood. After words ending in *ṣa*, *anubandha*, *bhida*, and so forth, the suffix *tvaḍ* (*tva*) is applied. Having thus set forth the sūtra that prescribes these two suffixes, *kāra* and *ī*, one should employ them in usage. However, for other feminine abstract suffixes (*bhāvapratyaya*), the genitive case is optionally used when the agent is expressed, as in: "The composition of the Sūtra by Śarvavarman is wonderful," and so on. Generally, the [rules regarding] the agent and the object are already stated;
the application of others has not been excluded, following their respective designations. (Verse 13)

For the most part—that is, in the majority of cases—the case endings for the agent (*kartṛ*) and the object (*karman*) are indeed seen as they have been stated. Therefore, those very [endings] being stated does not preclude the occurrence of other case endings according to their respective designations and without overstepping actual usage; rather, the intention is that they should proceed in accordance with usage. For example: "In the case of the object of a verb meaning 'to go,' the second and fourth [case endings] are used, provided there is physical movement and the word *adhvan* ('road') is not employed. [Examples: *grāmāya gacchati* (he goes to the village), *grāmaṃ gacchati* (he goes to the village), *grāmaṃ gantum* (in order to go to the village).

"To go to the village," and so forth—because of the association with the root *gam* (to go), only those verbal roots that take a single object are to be understood here. Therefore, in cases such as "he leads the goat to the village" (*grāmam ajāṃ nayati*), where there are multiple objects, the dative case does not occur. Likewise, regarding another object when disregard is expressed toward a living being: "I do not consider you a blade of grass" (*na tvāṃ tṛṇaṃ manye*) or "I do not consider you even a blade of grass" (*na tvāṃ tṛṇāya manye*). [The same applies] to the object of verbs meaning "to remember": "he remembers his mother" (*mātuḥ smarati*) or "he remembers his mother" (*mātaraṃ smarati*); "he studies from his mother" (*mātur adhyeti*) or "he studies from his mother" (*mātaram adhyeti*); "he causes his mother to remember" (*mātuḥ smarayati*).

One causes [someone] to remember their mother (*mātaraṃ smarayati*). For the purpose of remembering the mother, one uses forms such as *mātuḥ smartum* or *mātaraṃ smartum*. According to Pāṇini’s rule regarding improvement (*pratiyatna*)—as in *edhodakasyopaskartum* or *edhodakam upaskartum*—one likewise [uses the genitive]. Similarly, in the case of imitation (*anukaroti*), when Nārāyaṇa is the object, the second case is used: *nārāyaṇam anukaroti*; however, when there is a relationship with Nārāyaṇa, the sixth case is used. Likewise for verbs meaning "to harm" (*hiṃsārtha*)—excluding those beginning with *ad*—as in *dāsyā bhajati rogaḥ* ("the disease afflicts the female slave") or *dāsīm* ("the female slave"). Also, in the case of *caurasya ajñātayā* ("unknown to the thief") or *cauram* ("the thief"), and so forth.

Thus, as in the case of the roots *vyava-hṛ* ("to deal with") and *div* ("to play/dice") when used in the sense of transaction (*vyavahāra*): *śatasya vyavaharati* ("he deals with a hundred"), *śataṃ vyavaharati*; *śatasya dīvyati* ("he plays for a hundred"), *śataṃ vā*; *śatasya paṇāyate* ("he stakes a hundred"), *śataṃ vā*. Similarly, with the root *ā-śās* ("to wish/bless"): *sarpiṣām āśāste* ("he wishes for clarified butter"), *sarpir vā*. In these cases, beginning with *vyavaharati*, the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is to be understood for the object (*karman*) when there is an intention to express a relationship (*saṃbandha*).

Thus, when there is an intention to express the instrument (*karaṇa*) as the object (*karman*), and the recipient (*saṃpradāna*) as the object, [the following applies]: "In the case of *saṃjñā*, the third case ending is optionally used. For example: *putreṇa saṃjānīte* or *putraṃ saṃjānīte*. Similarly, when there is an intention to express the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) of that which has the sense of the past passive participle (*kta*), the seventh case ending is used. For example: *adhītī vyākaraṇe*. Here, the suffix *kta* is applied in the neuter gender in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāve*), denoting that "the study has been completed" (*adhyayanam adhītam*). Then, the suffix *in* is added in the sense of "one who possesses that" (*tad asyāsti*).
In this way, other case endings should also be understood according to the intended meaning. Thus, the distinction of case endings shown previously should be brought here and applied in this verse:

"The third [case] is used for the instrument (*karaṇa*); generally, the fourth is for the recipient (*saṃpradāna*). The fifth would be for the point of departure (*apādāna*), and likewise the seventh for the locus (*adhikaraṇa*). (14)

The third case (*tṛtīyā*) occurs in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇa*), the fourth (*caturthī*) in the sense of the recipient (*saṃpradāna*), the fifth (*pañcamī*) in the sense of the point of departure (*apādāna*), and likewise the seventh (*saptamī*) in the sense of the locus (*adhikaraṇa*). In the grammatical category of the instrument (*karaṇa-kāraka*), the third case generally occurs. Regarding the remaining cases, such as the object (*karman*) and the instrument (*karaṇa*), [it is said]: "That by which the agent acts, or by which the accomplishment of the agent's action is brought about—that *kāraka* which is intended as being proximate to the accomplishment of the agent's action is designated as the 'instrument' (*karaṇa*). That [instrument] is of two kinds.

"External and internal. Of these two, that which relies upon the body is internal; other than that is external. Among them, the internal is, for example: "he goes by mind," "seen by the eye. The external is, for example: "he cuts with a sickle," "he goes by horse," and so forth; thus, it is indicated that other case endings (*vibhakti*) are generally to be understood according to their respective expressions. For instance: "released by a little" (*stokena muktaḥ*), "released from a little" (*stokānmuktaḥ*); "released by a small amount" (*alpena muktaḥ*), "released from a small amount" (*alpānmuktaḥ*).

"Released from hardship with difficulty," "released by a few [days]," "released by some [time]. When there is no intention to express the duration of time (*kāla*) for the words *stoka*, *alpa*, *kṛcchra*, and *katipaya*, the fifth case (*pañcamī*) is used for the instrument (*karaṇa*). Similarly: *sarpiṣo jānīte* ("He knows [the taste] through clarified butter"). For the verb *jñā* meaning "to know," the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is used for the connection with the instrument. Such examples should be understood according to their specific grammatical expression. The phrase "the fourth case (*caturthī*) occurs due to the recipient (*saṃpradāna*)" is to be connected with each [preceding rule].

The remaining [kārakas], beginning with the "agent of action" (*karmakaraṇa*), are designated as the recipient (*saṃpradāna*) when there is a desire to give to someone out of a wish to honor or favor them. This is threefold, according to the rule "to whom one gives," etc.: the consenter (*anumaṃtṛ*), the rejecter (*nirākartṛ*), and the instigator (*preraka*). (It is proclaimed that the recipient of the verb *dadāti* is the cause of relinquishment, which is reached through the pervasion [of the intention]). For example, when it is said, "I give this," and [the other] says, "Do so," he is a consenter. As in: "He gives a cow to the teacher."

That which, having uttered "give," impels the giver, is *preraka* (impelling). For example: "He gives alms to the student. That which neither approves nor impels, but rather does not reject, is *anirākartṛ* (non-rejecting). It remains silent. For example: "He gives a garland to the Buddha. Here too, there is a connection with the word "mostly" (*prāyaśaḥ*). "The lover bestows gold upon her"—here the *ātmanepada* ending is used because the root *dāṇ* (to give) is used in the sense of the dative case.

In the case of an improper practice (*aśiṣṭasamācāra*), the third case ending is used for the recipient (*saṃpradāna*) when there is an intention to express it as the instrument (*karaṇa*). One should understand that in other instances as well, the distinction of case endings occurs according to the specific expression. The fifth case ending (*pañcamī*) is used for the ablative (*apādāna*), and likewise, the seventh case ending (*saptamī*) is used for the locus (*adhikaraṇa*). (14)

"The fifth [case-ending] occurs in the sense of *apādāna* (the point of departure). By the rule "the remaining [cases are used for] object, instrument," etc., and by the rule "from which one departs," the fifth case is employed for the *apādāna*. The technical term *apādāna* applies to a *kāraka* (grammatical participant) that is intended as a limit or boundary. That [limit] is of two kinds: moving and non-moving. Among these, an example of the moving is: "He fell from a running horse. An example of the non-moving is: "The leaf falls from the tree. Likewise: "He fears the tiger."

Expressions such as "he studies under the preceptor" (upādhyāyād adhīte) should be understood as having the nature of a limit (avadhi). Now, one might ask: how is it that the genitive case is used in "the leaf of the tree falls" (vṛkṣasya parṇaṃ patati)? True; for this is intended to express a relationship (saṃbandha), and it has been shown that by such an intention, the factors of action (kāraka) arise. For example: "He cooks in a pot," "He cooks with a pot," and "Devadatta cooks with a pot. In such instances, a single [object] is seen to be expressed in various ways according to the speaker's intention.

Furthermore, when an agent attributes his own activity to an action that is being performed without effort, then—by virtue of the speaker's intention—the object becomes the agent. For example: *pacyate odanaḥ svayam eva* (the rice cooks by itself), *alāti kedāraḥ svayam eva* (the field receives [water] by itself), and so forth. Because the object functions as the agent, this is called "object-as-agent" (*karmakartṛ*). Due to the status of being like the object (*karmavadbhāva*), the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is used. When that occurs, the *yaṇ* and *iv* [substitutions] take place. Thus, in *odane* and so on, the nominative case is used because the object has been expressed. *pacelimā taṇḍulāḥ svayam eva* (the rice grains are such that they cook by themselves).

In the case of a *karmakartṛ* (an agent who is simultaneously the object), the term applies to a *kevalin* (one who has attained absolute knowledge). The inclusion of the particle *vat* is for the sake of including its own substratum; thus, even in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*), the usage of a *karmakartṛ* indeed occurs. For example: *pacyate odanena svayameva* ("the rice cooks by itself"). Because [the *karmakartṛ*] is not explicitly mentioned [as such], the status of being "like the object" (*karmavadbhāva*) does not apply within the section on *kṛt* suffixes. Consequently, *kṛt* suffixes prescribed for the object do not occur when the agent is the *karmakartṛ*. Examples: *kartavyaṃ kaṭena svayameva* ("the mat must be made by itself") and *īṣatkaraḥ kaṭena svayameva* ("the mat is easily made by itself").

Thus, it is established that the specific rule concerning the agent of the action (*karmakartṛ*) is to be understood there. Likewise, the locative case (*saptamī*) is used for the locus (*ādhāra*). "Likewise" means "it should be so. Regarding the remaining [cases], by the rule beginning with *karmakaraṇa* (and including *ādhāre saptamī*, *ādhāraśca*), the locus (*ādhāra*)—which is the substratum of the action—is that upon which the agent or the object is supported, where the agent and the object abide. That which is the locus is called the "locus" (*adhikaraṇa*); thus, the locus receives the technical designation of "locus. And that is of four kinds.

[The locative relation] is of four kinds: based on contact (*upaśleṣika*), based on pervasion (*abhivyāpika*), based on the object (*vaiṣayika*), and based on proximity (*sāmīpika*). Among these, *upaśleṣa* is conjunction; that which exists therein is *upaśleṣika*. For example: "Devadatta sits on a mat. Likewise: "He cooks rice in a pot. That which exists pervading its receptacle is *abhivyāpaka*; for example: "There is oil in sesame seeds. The object (*viṣaya*) is the range [of perception], the state of not existing elsewhere; that which exists therein is *vaiṣayika*; for example: "The gods are in heaven. That which exists in the vicinity or nearness is *sāmīpika*;
for example: "There is a hamlet on the Ganges. This applies everywhere in the same way.

Now, regarding the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) used in the sense of relation (*saṃbandha*), such is the established conclusion. Through the investigation of what has been stated and what remains to be said, let the usage be understood accordingly. By the rule beginning with "the remainder [is the genitive] for the object, the instrument," and so forth, the genitive is used for relation, as in: *rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ* (the king's man), *yuvayoḥ putraḥ* (the son of you two), *yuṣmākaṃ dhanam* (your wealth), and so on. In these instances, there exists a relation produced by a single action; and that [relation] is said to consist of mutual dependence.

For instance, in the expression "the king's man," the relationship between these two is established by the action of protection; for the king protects and the man is protected. When it is said, "The king has gone to protect," there arises an expectation for a specific object, and thus the king becomes related to the man. When it is said, "The man is being protected," there is an intention to specify the agent, and thus the man becomes related to the king. In this manner, the relationship should be understood everywhere.

Furthermore, there exists a relationship of mutual dependence between both [terms]. If that is so, why is the genitive case not used after the word *puruṣa* as well, just as it is after the word *rājan*? True; even in cases such as "Devadatta cooks rice in a pot with wood," a relationship consisting of mutual dependence exists everywhere according to the manner already stated. Thus, how can the genitive case apply to each individual [term] here? Now, one might say: "[It] certainly exists in all cases."

Even if there were indeed an individual connection [between each], it is still not intended to be expressed in that way. Since at that time the meaning of the agent (*kartṛ*) and so forth is what is intended to be expressed (*vivakṣita*), and a word is employed only when it denotes the meaning intended to be expressed, how could there be the contingency of the genitive case? If this is so, then here too, since the meaning of the gender (*liṅga*) is primary as the object to be conveyed, the nominative alone follows after the word *puruṣa*, and not the genitive; for even though a relationship exists, it is not intended to be expressed.

Therefore it has been said: "The connection between the qualified (bhedya) and the qualifier (bhedaka) is desired as a mutual conjunction (*śliṣṭi*). Although this connection resides in both, the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) arises from the qualifier. Consequently, it is established that a word expressive of that [intended] meaning is employed when that meaning is intended to be conveyed. For this very reason, because of the intention to convey [a specific sense], this principle is proclaimed everywhere: in all cases, the singular number is used for one object, the dual number for two objects, and the plural number for many objects.

This should be understood through the force of the literal meaning (*anvarthabala*). However, in a case of grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇa*), the qualifier and the qualified share a single case ending; as it has been said:
"Whatever gender, number, and case-endings are seen in the qualified [word], they are applied to the qualifier as well."

Generally, those same [words] become the agent (*kartṛ*) when they function as qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*) with the same meaning. For example: *kaṭaḥ kriyate darśanīyo vipulaḥ* ("A beautiful, large mat is being made"). Because of the connection with each [qualifier] individually, the nominative case (*prathamā*) is used. This principle should be understood to apply everywhere. For example: *kaṭau kriyete darśanīyau vipulau* ("Two beautiful, large mats are being made"); *kaṭāḥ kriyante darśanīyāḥ vipulāḥ* ("Beautiful, large mats are being made"). Likewise: *karoti kaṭaṃ darśanīyaṃ vipulam* ("He makes a beautiful, large mat"); *devadattena kṛtaḥ* ("Made by Devadatta"); *brāhmaṇāya vedapāragāya gāṃ dehi* ("Give a cow to the Brahmin who has mastered the Vedas").

A leaf falls from a large tree. A man [belongs] to an aged king. There are birds in the pervasive sky. In this way, the dual and plural numbers are also to be understood. If this is so, how is it that one says, "twenty mats are being made"? True; by its very nature, this word *viṃśati* ends only in the singular, and thus it takes on only the case-ending of the substantive. Other instances should be understood in the same way.

[Objection: But even so, since [the action] is performed, how can there be the plural number, given that "twenty" (*viṃśati*) ends in the singular? [Response: There is no such fault, because it is connected with the word ending in the plural, namely *kaṭāḥ* ("mats"). [Objection: Let it be so; let it not be otherwise. Nevertheless, the connection of the verb with each [individual] was demonstrated immediately prior. Therefore, due to its connection with the word "twenty," the singular would also follow. It is not only due to the connection with *kaṭāḥ* that the plural occurs.

It is true that because the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) is predominant, [the suffix] takes its number alone; as in the example, "the threads are made into a cloth," where the number of the material cause (*prakṛti*) is used because of its predominance. For here, the threads are the material cause. The modification (*vikāra*), however—the cloth—is subordinate because it is rooted in them. This same principle should be stated for *kṛt*, *taddhita*, and compound formations as well. For example: "twenty mats have been purchased" (*viṃśatiḥ kaṭāḥ krītāḥ*); "twenty grammarians" (*viṃśatir vaiyākaraṇāḥ*).

In expressions such as *viṃśatiḥ puruṣāḥ kṛtapraṇāmāḥ* ("twenty men who have performed prostrations"), one should understand that the gender and number of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) are those of the substantive (*viśeṣya*), provided they are in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*). However, in cases such as *pradhānaṃ puruṣaḥ* ("the primary person"), because the word *pradhāna* is indeclinable in gender (*aviṣṭaliṅgatva*), words like *pradhāna* do not take on the gender of the substantive. For this very reason, it was stated in the section beginning with "gender and number" (*liṅgasaṃkhyā*) that this is generally the case. Thus, having explained what has been stated and what has not been stated, and having shown the case endings to be understood, he states the rule: "The determination is indeed of this kind; therefore, let the usage be understood through the investigation of what has been stated and what has not been stated."

"By means of the investigation of what has been stated and what has not been stated, let the formal application (*prayoga*) be understood. The word "tāvat" refers to the sequence; by that [sequence], let the formal application be understood through the investigation of what has been stated and what has not been stated. Let the sentence in the form of "A mat is being made by Devadatta," which is characterized by the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*), be understood; that is, let it be explained—meaning, let it be formulated—by the students. This is the form of the root *gam* with the suffix *in*.

In the verse stating that "the employment of a term whose meaning is already understood is a matter of personal choice," it was not specified [that this applies] "to students. For example, the expression "this mountain is Sumeru" is such a usage. In that context, *sādhya* (the thing to be accomplished) refers to the action, which is the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*). That by which the action is accomplished through its various components is the *sādhana* (means of accomplishment), namely the six types of factors (*kāraka*). As it has been said: "A factor (*kāraka*) is established in common worldly usage as the cause of action. Furthermore, that collection of words by which both the thing to be accomplished and the means of accomplishment are conveyed must be called a *vākya* (sentence).

For it is from that alone—namely, from the sentence—that linguistic usage proceeds, because only that, by virtue of being free from expectancy (*nirākāṅkṣatā*), serves as the cause for engagement or withdrawal. For example, a sentence such as "One desiring heaven should perform the *agnihotra* sacrifice" is a cause for engagement; a sentence such as "A Brahmin must not be killed" is a cause for withdrawal. And yet, the status of being a cause for engagement or withdrawal is never observed in an isolated word.

Therefore, knowing that verbal discourse being carried out by many must be performed by means of words (*pada*), yet fearing that people of dull intellect might occasionally doubt the establishment of individual words when composing many of them, [the author], while illuminating the connection between grammatical factors (*kāraka*), says: "This effort of ours, directed toward them, is already established. "Having mastered this four-hundred-verse work joined with twenty [additional verses], may the world proceed with alacrity through the accomplishment of the illumination of the connection (*saṃbandhodyota*)."
Thus concludes the *Saṃbandhodyota*, also known by the name *Ṣaṭkāraka*, composed by Rabhasananda through [the exposition of] the six grammatical relations.

The wise should thus tolerate even that which is deficient in syllables, words, or vowels, or where the euphonic combinations (*saṃdhi*) have increased the letter *r*; for who does not become bewildered by the ocean of the scriptures?
The *Ṣaṭkāraka* composed by Rabhasananda was written down.
